items.title: Why a client import of the service fails the build
items.body:
`server/services/catalog.ts` starts with `import "server-only"`. If a Client Component imports that module, the build stops with an error instead of quietly bundling server code into the browser. The file's own comment calls this one of the two guards on the client and server seam; the ESLint layering rule is the other.

- Waiting for Prisma to throw in the browser would mean the code already shipped; the guard works earlier, at build time.
- Next.js does not automatically strip server code from a client bundle; anything a client file imports is bundled.
- TypeScript has no rule against async functions in client files; the protection comes from `server-only`.

excerpts.quote: import "server-only";
If a Client Component // imports this module, `server-only` makes the BUILD fail with a clear message instead of // silently bundling server code

readMore.why: How the boundary is enforced: the lint rule, server-only and the service tests.

items.title: Why cents become text only in formatMoney
items.body:
The money rule says: do every calculation on the integer, and turn it into a display string exactly once, at the edge. In Storefront that one place is `formatMoney` in `lib/money.ts`, which hands the cents to `Intl.NumberFormat`. ADR-0002 names it the single place cents becomes a display string.

- Calling `toFixed(2)` in each component would spread formatting everywhere, and `.toFixed` is one of the shapes the fitness test forbids.
- The service view-model carries a `Money` value, not a string, so the UI can still format it consistently.
- The repository returns Prisma rows with integer `priceCents`; the database never stores formatted strings.

excerpts.quote: Do all arithmetic on the integer. Convert to a display string exactly once, at the > edge.
**`formatMoney(money)` is the single place cents becomes a display string** (via `Intl.NumberFormat`).

items.title: Why Cents is a branded number
items.body:
A branded type is a normal `number` at runtime with an extra compile-time tag. Because a plain number lacks the tag, TypeScript refuses `const price: Cents = 1999`; the only way to get a `Cents` is through `money()`, which also checks the integer rule. That stops a dollar amount or a stray arithmetic result from posing as money.

- Prisma does not require branded types; it maps `Int` columns to plain numbers.
- JSON serialization is unchanged; a branded number serializes as a number, not a string.
- Branding changes nothing at runtime; it is erased by the compiler, so there is no 64-bit integer either.

excerpts.quote: `Cents` is a `number` at runtime but a distinct type at // compile time, so a raw `number` cannot be passed where `Cents` is expected
export type Cents = number & { readonly __brand: "Cents" };

readMore.why: The rejected unbranded alternative and why the brand is nearly free.

items.title: Why a missing onError leaves a phantom cart item
items.body:
An optimistic update changes the cart cache before the server answers. `onMutate` takes a snapshot and applies the change; `onError` is the step that puts the snapshot back. If `onError` is not wired, a 409 from the server changes nothing on screen: the item stays in the drawer and the badge stays wrong until a hard refresh reloads real data.

- The item does not disappear by itself; nothing removes it without a rollback.
- No toast or automatic removal happens unless your code adds it.
- TanStack Query does not restore the previous cache for you; the restore is the code you write in `onError`.

excerpts.quote: the server returns 409; `onError` isn't wired. The item stays in the drawer, the badge stays at 3, the total is wrong — until a hard refresh.
**`onError`** — restore the snapshot. This is the line that gets forgotten, because the happy path looks perfect without it.

readMore.why: The full three-moment pattern with code.

items.title: Why the three shares are 334, 333 and 333
items.body:
Whole cents cannot split 1000 into three equal parts: three shares of 333 add up to 999, so one cent would vanish. `allocate` uses **largest-remainder** allocation: it floors every share first, then gives the leftover cents one at a time to the shares with the largest remainders. Here one cent is left over, so exactly one share becomes 334 and the total is exactly 1000.

- *333, 333, 333* is the floored result before the leftover cent is handed out; it loses a cent.
- *334, 334, 332* also sums to 1000, but shares never differ by more than one cent, and nothing is taken away from a share.
- *333.33 each* is not possible: `money()` rejects non-integer cents.

excerpts.quote: You cannot split 1000¢ into 3 equal integer shares — // 333+333+333 = 999, a penny vanishes. Floor each share, then hand the leftover units one by // one to the largest remainders.
const share = Math.floor((total_ * w) / weightSum);

readMore.why: The full allocate function, including how leftover cents are ordered.

items.title: Concept: money is a whole number of cents
items.body:
Computers store most decimal fractions like 0.1 only approximately. Add a few approximate numbers and the error grows until an order total is a cent off. Storefront avoids the problem by never storing dollars at all: a price is an **integer number of cents**, so `$19.99` is `1999`.

`lib/money.ts` is where that rule is turned into code. Read it top to bottom; it is short and every function has a comment saying why it exists. As you read, answer these from the code rather than from memory:

- What is a `Money` value made of, and what is special about the `Cents` type? Look up "branded type" if the term is new.
- What does the `money()` constructor do with an amount before it builds a value, and what happens to an amount it does not accept?
- Where, and in how many places, are cents turned into text like `$19.99`?
- How does `allocate` split an amount that does not divide evenly?

Then read the **Consequences** section of ADR-0002 to see how the rule is checked automatically by a fitness test, a test that scans source text instead of running the code. Note exactly which folders it scans.

excerpts.quote: Represent money as an **integer count of the currency's smallest unit** — cents for USD — carried in > a `Money` value. Do all arithmetic on the integer.

readMore.why: The whole money kit in one file: the constructor, the arithmetic helpers and the formatter.
The decision record: what was chosen, what it costs, and the alternatives that were rejected.

items.title: Why three same-price variants read as a flat $25.00
items.body:
The service decides whether a card shows a price range. It puts every variant's `priceCents` into a `Set` and checks whether the set holds more than one value. Three variants at 2500 cents give a set with one value, so `priceVaries` is false and the card shows the cheapest price as a plain **$25.00**.

- *From $25.00* is the wording for a real range; it needs at least two distinct prices.
- *$75.00* adds the variants together, but a card shows the price of one item, not of the whole set.
- *No price until a variant is picked* is not how the list card works: `price` is always the cheapest variant's price.

excerpts.quote: const priceVaries = new Set(p.variants.map((v) => v.priceCents)).size > 1;
A multi-variant product whose variants all cost the same is NOT a range.

readMore.why: The unit tests that pin the from-price behaviour without a database.

items.title: Why ProductListItem leaves variant attributes out
items.body:
ADR-0003 keeps the view-model but adds a narrow rule: do not pre-map fields that no screen uses yet. Variant `attributes` (size and colour) are in the schema and the seed from S02 because S03 needs them, but no S02 screen renders them, so the S02 list item does not carry them. The DTO grows when a screen needs a field.

- The ESLint layering rule is about which folders may import which; it says nothing about JSON columns.
- The omission is deliberate and documented, not a bug a later sprint flags.
- Size is not the reason; view-models are small plain values and attributes would serialize fine.

excerpts.quote: Keep the view-model, **but do not pre-map fields no screen uses yet.** The DTO grows when a > screen needs a field, not speculatively.
S03's variant picker is the first screen that renders them. Deliberate, not gold-plated.

items.title: Why formatMoney's divide does not trip the fitness test
items.body:
The fitness test is a plain text scan, and it only looks inside one folder. `SCAN_DIR` is `server/`, and `formatMoney` lives in `lib/money.ts`, so its single `/ 100` is never read by the scan. That is deliberate: the rule bans float money math in server code while the formatter owns the one allowed divide, for display only.

- The regex is not limited to `/ 100.0`; it matches a slash, optional spaces and `100` not followed by another digit, so a plain `/ 100` would be caught under `server/`.
- There is no whitelist for lines that mention `Intl.NumberFormat`; the scan does not care what a line means.
- The test does fail: it uses `expect(...).toEqual([])`, so any violation turns the run red.

excerpts.quote: const SCAN_DIR = join(ROOT, "server");
`formatMoney` owns the single deliberate `/ 100`, and it // lives in `lib/`, not `server/`.

readMore.why: The whole scan: the forbidden patterns and how violations are reported.

items.title: Start here: four one-pagers, two ADRs, one seam
items.body:
Storefront is a teaching repo: a real Next.js shop whose docs explain *why* each piece of the code is shaped the way it is. Its thesis is that the server owns the truth and the client owns the experience, and most real bugs live at the seam between them.

Read in this order:

1. `docs/concepts/money-in-minor-units.md`, then `docs/adr/ADR-0002-money-in-minor-units.md` (how prices are stored and added).
2. `docs/concepts/data-boundary.md`, then `docs/adr/ADR-0003-view-models-at-the-service-boundary.md` (what the UI is allowed to see).
3. `docs/concepts/rsc-vs-client.md` (which components run in the browser).
4. `docs/concepts/optimistic-ui.md` (showing a change before the server confirms it).

Each one-pager ends with a **Try it** list. Do at least one item per page: the quiz asks you to *predict* behaviour, and predicting is much easier once you have watched the code do it. When a doc names a file such as `lib/money.ts` or `server/services/catalog.ts`, open it next to the doc. The comments in those files repeat the rule in context.

excerpts.quote: The server owns the truth; the client owns the experience — and the seam between them is where
**Prices, totals, tax, and stock are computed on the server, from the database.** A number that arrives from the browser is display state, never authority.

readMore.why: The course overview: what the shop does and how the 15 sprints are organised.
The first one-pager to read; the money rule everything else builds on.

items.title: Why use client on the page bloats the bundle
items.body:
`"use client"` marks a boundary: that file and everything it imports become client code that is sent to the browser. Put it on the products page and the whole subtree under the page joins the client bundle, even the parts that only render markup. The rule is to push the directive down and mark the small interactive piece, such as the filter dropdown, instead.

- The page is still rendered on the server for the first load; client components hydrate afterwards.
- The directive is not limited to one file's own code; it pulls in what that file renders and imports.
- Server data can still be passed as props; the cost is bundle size, not an empty page.

excerpts.quote: **Push `"use client"` down.** Marking a big layout client-side drags its whole subtree into the bundle. Mark the *button*, not the page.
On the server for the first render, then **hydrates and runs in the browser**

readMore.why: A small client island in the real code, with its server parent passing props.

items.title: Why a Server Component calls the service directly
items.body:
A Server Component already runs on the server, right next to `server/services`. Calling `listProducts()` is an ordinary function call. Calling `fetch("/api/products")` instead sends an HTTP request out and back to the same server, a round-trip to yourself that adds latency and a second code path for nothing.

- The one-pager does not say route handlers cannot be cached; caching is not the reason given.
- `fetch` is available in Server Components; the problem is the needless hop, not a missing API.
- Calling the service directly is not about skipping authentication. The service is server code either way, and authorization belongs in the service or action, not only in an API route.

excerpts.quote: Call the `server/services` function directly — it's already on the server. `fetch("/api/...")` from a server component is a round-trip to yourself.

readMore.why: The full list of rules that keep the server/client boundary honest.

items.title: Concept: rows in, view-models out, and where code runs
items.body:
Storefront reads data through three layers. `server/data` talks to the database with Prisma and returns rows. `server/services` turns those rows into small plain objects called **view-models** (or DTOs). The pages and components in `app/` and `components/` only ever render view-models.

Why bother? A database row has the database's shape: nullable joins, aggregate objects, column names. If the UI reads rows directly, every rename in the schema becomes a UI change. The service maps a row once, in a few explicit lines, and every screen reuses that one shape.

The second idea is *where code runs*. In the Next.js App Router every component runs on the server unless its file starts with `"use client"`. Server components can wait for data and ship no JavaScript; client components can hold state and handle clicks, but they are sent to the browser. Read `docs/concepts/data-boundary.md` first, then `docs/concepts/rsc-vs-client.md`, and keep `server/services/catalog.ts` open beside them.

excerpts.quote: Storefront reads data through three layers: `server/data` → `server/services` → the UI. Each has one job, and the value of the split is what it *stops* leaking.
Server Components are the **page and its data**. Client Components are the **interactive islands** > inside it.

readMore.why: The decision behind the service mapping, including the reviewer's pushback that limited it.
The real mapping code the data-boundary one-pager summarises.

items.title: Why an unflagged product still shows its first image
items.body:
The service picks the image with one line: the image flagged `isPrimary`, otherwise the first image, otherwise `null`. With two images and no flag, the first check finds nothing, so the second one returns `images[0]`.

- `null` is only for a product with no images at all; that is the last fallback in the chain.
- The service never invents a placeholder URL. When the image is `null` the card renders its own placeholder, but that is a UI choice, not data.
- The view-model has a single `image` field, so it can never carry both images.

excerpts.quote: const primary = p.images.find((img) => img.isPrimary) ?? p.images[0] ?? null;
The primary image, or `null` — the card renders a graceful placeholder when null.

items.title: Why money(1999 * 0.0825) throws
items.body:
`1999 * 0.0825` is about 164.92, which is not a whole number. The `money()` constructor checks `Number.isInteger` and throws instead of accepting it. That throw is the guardrail: it tells you float math happened upstream. The fix is to round the tax once, deliberately, in integers, for example `Math.round(1999 * 0.0825)`, and pass the result to `money()`.

- Nothing stores 164.9175; the value is rejected before a `Money` exists, so `formatMoney` never sees it.
- The constructor does not round silently; silent rounding is exactly what the rule avoids.
- TypeScript accepts the call: `money()` takes a plain `number` and the check happens at runtime.

excerpts.quote: if (!Number.isInteger(amountCents)) {
this throw is the guardrail. If you ever see it, something upstream did float // math (a `* 0.0825` tax without a `Math.round`, a `/ 100`) — fix it there, in integers.

readMore.why: The Try it list includes this exact tax calculation.
